title: My Feelings and My Choices
notes: Everyone has feelings. They can help us notice what is happening, but we can still choose what to do next. In this level, you will practice calming pauses, focusing again, and noticing what you do well.
summary: Notice how you feel, take a breath, and choose one helpful next step.
dailyHabits: Take three slow breaths when you feel rushed.
Notice one thing you did well.

modules.title: Notice Your Feelings
modules.challenge: For three days, pause when you feel worried, upset, or excited. Take three slow breaths and tell a trusted grown-up what you noticed.

microLessons.title: Pause and name it
microLessons.objective: Name a feeling and choose a kind, safe next step.
microLessons.body:
Feelings are clues. You might feel excited before a game or worried before a test. You can say, “I feel worried,” without saying that you are bad or wrong.

Pause, take three slow breaths, name the feeling, and choose what could help. You might ask for help, get a drink of water, or try one small step.
microLessons.audioScript: Pause for a moment. Take a slow breath. What are you feeling? What is one helpful thing you can do next?
microLessons.imagePrompt: A cheerful primary school student taking three calm breaths before starting a classroom activity

task.description: Think of one feeling you had today. Name it and choose one helpful thing to do.

microLessons.journalPrompt: What feeling did you notice today? What helped you?

quiz.prompt: What can you do when a big feeling arrives?
options: Pause, name it, and choose a helpful step

microLessons.title: Bring your mind back
microLessons.objective: Practice returning your attention to one task.
microLessons.body:
Sometimes our minds wander while we read, listen, or do homework. That happens to everyone. When you notice, take one breath and bring your mind back to the next small part.

You can point to the line you are reading, put away one distraction, or ask a grown-up for a quiet place. Each time you return, you are practicing focus.
microLessons.audioScript: If your mind wanders, that is okay. Notice it, take one breath, and come back to the next small part.
microLessons.imagePrompt: A young student reading at a bright desk with a pencil and a small plant

task.description: Read or work on one thing for five minutes. When your mind wanders, gently come back.

microLessons.journalPrompt: What helps you pay attention when you read or learn?

quiz.prompt: What can you do when you notice your mind wandered?

modules.title: My Strengths and Dreams
modules.challenge: Draw or write one thing you would like to learn. Ask someone you trust to help you choose one small step to try this week.

microLessons.title: What matters to me?
microLessons.objective: Notice a strength or kind value you want to practice.
microLessons.body:
People are good at different things. You might be patient, curious, brave, helpful, or good at making others laugh. These are strengths you can use to learn and help.

Think of a time you felt proud of something you did. What strength did you use? Choose one strength to practice today, such as sharing, trying again, or listening carefully.
microLessons.audioScript: Think of one thing you do well. How could you use that strength to learn or help someone today?
microLessons.imagePrompt: A group of diverse primary students sharing drawings that show their different strengths

task.description: Draw or write one thing you do well. Show it to a trusted person and ask what they notice about your strengths.

microLessons.journalPrompt: What is one thing you do well, and how can you use it to help?

options: Something helpful you can do or practice
A reason to be better than others

microLessons.title: One step toward my dream
microLessons.objective: Turn a learning wish into one small action.
microLessons.body:
A dream can be something you hope to learn or do. Maybe you want to read a bigger book, learn a sport, or help care for a garden. You do not have to do it all today.

Pick one small step. You could read one page, practice for five minutes, or ask someone how to begin. Small steps help dreams grow, just like little drops fill a bucket.
microLessons.audioScript: Choose something you want to learn. What is one small step you can try today?
microLessons.imagePrompt: A child taking a small stepping stone toward a colorful path through green hills

task.description: Write or draw something you want to learn. Choose one small step to try today.

microLessons.journalPrompt: What would you like to learn? What is your first small step?

quiz.prompt: Which is a small first step toward learning to draw?
options: Wait until you are an artist
Give up if it looks tricky

questions.prompt: What can you do when you notice a strong feeling?
options: Pause, name it, and choose a helpful step

questions.prompt: What can help when your mind wanders?
options: Come back gently to the next small part

questions.prompt: How can you begin a dream?
Name one strength you have and one way you can use it this week.

title: Little Habits, Big Growth
notes: A habit is something we practice again and again. Small habits can help us learn, care for ourselves, and keep our promises. In this level, you will make a tiny plan, focus on one task, and try again when a day does not go as planned.
summary: Start small, practice often, and try again when things get tricky.
dailyHabits: Put your learning things in one place.
Start one task for five minutes.
Notice one thing you tried today.

modules.title: Small Habits That Stick
modules.challenge: Choose one helpful habit, such as reading or packing your school bag. Practice it for five days and mark each day you try. Ask a grown-up to help you remember.

microLessons.title: Start very small
microLessons.objective: Make a habit easy to remember and begin.
microLessons.body:
A big job can feel hard to start. Make the first part small. Instead of “read a whole book,” try “read one page after dinner.” Instead of “clean everything,” put away five things.

Choose when you will do it and connect it to something you already do. A small start can grow as you keep practicing.
microLessons.audioScript: Choose one helpful habit. Make the first step small and choose when you will do it.
microLessons.imagePrompt: A child checking off a simple five-day reading habit chart

task.description: Pick a helpful habit. Write or draw the tiny first step and when you will do it.

microLessons.journalPrompt: What small habit would you like to practice this week?

quiz.prompt: Which is the easiest habit to begin?

microLessons.title: Get ready to begin
microLessons.objective: Prepare a space or reminder that makes a helpful habit easier.
microLessons.body:
Getting ready can make a task easier. Put your book and pencil where you can find them. Pack your school bag before bedtime. Ask a grown-up to help you set a reminder.

You do not need a perfect room. Choose one small change that helps you begin. Put away one toy or turn off one distraction while you work.
microLessons.audioScript: Make it easier to begin. Put what you need nearby and move one distraction out of the way.
microLessons.imagePrompt: A cozy, simple study corner with a school book, pencil case, and packed bag

task.description: Get one thing ready for a task you want to do tomorrow.

microLessons.journalPrompt: What could you get ready today to help tomorrow-you?

quiz.prompt: What can help you start homework?
options: Put your book and pencil nearby

modules.title: Focus and Try Again
modules.challenge: Choose one school or home task. Work on it for five minutes, take a short stretch break, then try another five minutes. If you forget, begin again the next day.

microLessons.title: One thing at a time
microLessons.objective: Break a big task into small parts and focus on one part.
microLessons.body:
A big task can feel like a mountain. Break it into little steps. For a school project, you might choose a topic, draw a picture, and write one sentence.

Pick just the next step. Work on it for five minutes, then pause. You can ask your teacher or a grown-up if you are not sure what to do.
microLessons.audioScript: When a task feels big, choose the very next small part. Do that part first.
microLessons.imagePrompt: A child climbing a friendly illustrated hill made of small colorful stepping stones

task.description: Choose a task. Draw or write its first small step, then work on that step for five minutes.

microLessons.journalPrompt: What big task feels easier after you break it into little steps?

quiz.prompt: What can you do when a task feels too big?

microLessons.title: Try again tomorrow
microLessons.objective: Use a missed day as a chance to make a new plan.
microLessons.body:
Sometimes we forget a habit or cannot finish a task. That happens to everyone. It does not mean you cannot learn.

Ask yourself: “What got in the way?” Maybe you needed help, more time, or a reminder. Make one small change and try again. You can ask a trusted grown-up for help.
microLessons.audioScript: If a plan did not work today, that is okay. Think of one change and try again.
microLessons.imagePrompt: A child smiling while reopening a book after a rainy day, with sunlight coming through a window

task.description: Think of one plan that did not happen. Draw or write one way to make it easier next time.

microLessons.journalPrompt: What helps you try again when something feels hard?

quiz.prompt: If you miss a day of your habit, what can you do?
options: Try again and make a helpful change

questions.prompt: How can you make a new habit easier?
options: Wait until you never feel tired
Try to do everything at once

questions.prompt: What can help you focus on a big task?
options: Think about every part at once

questions.prompt: What can you do after missing a habit?
options: Try again and make a new plan

questions.prompt: Name one helpful habit you want to practice. When will you try it?

title: Kind Choices and Teamwork
notes: We learn and play with other people. Listening, using kind words, and thinking about what is fair can help everyone feel included. In this level, you will practice teamwork and small ways to help at home or school.
summary: Listen carefully, use kind words, and help your group work together.
dailyHabits: Let someone finish speaking before you answer.
Use kind words when you disagree.
Offer one helpful action at home or school.

modules.title: Listening and Kind Words
modules.challenge: During one conversation or game this week, let another person finish, say what you heard, and ask if you understood. Try to include someone who has not had a turn.

microLessons.title: Listen with care
microLessons.objective: Show someone you are listening and check what they mean.
microLessons.body:
Listening means giving someone a chance to finish. Look toward them if that feels comfortable. Then say one thing you heard: “You wanted a turn too.” You can ask, “Did I understand?”

People may like different games or have different ideas. Listening helps you learn what they think. You do not have to agree with everything to be kind.
microLessons.audioScript: Let the other person finish. Say what you heard and ask if you understood.
microLessons.imagePrompt: Two primary school children taking turns to talk and listen in a sunny school garden

task.description: In one conversation, let someone finish and tell them one thing you heard.

microLessons.journalPrompt: How do you feel when someone listens to you?

quiz.prompt: What is one way to show you are listening?

microLessons.title: Use kind words when you disagree
microLessons.objective: Tell someone what you need without using hurtful words.
microLessons.body:
Friends do not always agree. You can talk about a problem without calling someone a name. Try saying what happened and what you need.

You could say, “I felt sad when I did not get a turn. Can I have the next turn?” Listen to what the other person says. If you feel unsafe or someone keeps hurting you, tell a trusted grown-up.
microLessons.audioScript: You can disagree and still be kind. Say what happened, say what you need, and ask a trusted grown-up for help if you feel unsafe.
microLessons.imagePrompt: Two classmates kindly solving a disagreement about taking turns with a ball

task.description: Practice one kind sentence you could use when you need a turn or need help.

microLessons.journalPrompt: What kind words could you use if you and a friend want different things?

quiz.prompt: Which sentence uses kind words to solve a problem?
options: Can I have a turn next?
I will never play with you

modules.title: Fair Choices and Helping
modules.challenge: Choose one safe way to help at home or school. Ask first, do the helpful task, and thank the person who worked with you.

microLessons.title: Pause and think about what is fair
microLessons.objective: Think about safety, fairness, and other people before choosing.
microLessons.body:
Before you choose, pause and ask: “Is it safe? Is it fair? How might another person feel?” These questions can help with games, sharing, and group work.

If you are not sure, stop and ask a trusted grown-up. You can change your choice when you learn something new. Good choices help keep people safe and included.
microLessons.audioScript: Before you choose, think about safety, fairness, and how another person might feel.
microLessons.imagePrompt: Children sharing colorful art supplies fairly at a classroom table

task.description: Think of a small choice today. Ask yourself whether it is safe and fair to everyone.

microLessons.journalPrompt: What is one way to make a game or group activity fair for everyone?

quiz.prompt: What can you ask before making a choice?
options: Will I always get my way?

microLessons.title: Help your group
microLessons.objective: Offer a helpful action and give others a chance to join in.
microLessons.body:
Helping does not mean doing everything by yourself. Ask, “Would you like help?” You could share supplies, tidy a play area, or help a classmate find a page.

Good teamwork gives everyone a turn. Thank people for helping you too. If a job is not safe or you are unsure, ask a grown-up first.
microLessons.audioScript: Ask if someone would like help. Share the work, let everyone take a turn, and ask a grown-up if you are unsure.
microLessons.imagePrompt: A small group of children working together to tidy a classroom garden

task.description: Ask someone at home or school if one small helpful job would make their day easier.

microLessons.journalPrompt: What is one way you can help your class, family, or friends this week?

quiz.prompt: What is a kind way to offer help?
options: Tell someone they cannot do it

questions.prompt: How can you show someone you are listening?
options: Let them finish and say what you heard

questions.prompt: What can you say when you need a turn?
options: Can I have the next turn?

questions.prompt: What can help you make a fair choice?
options: Think about safety and other people

questions.prompt: What is one safe way you can help someone at home or school?
